voiceover.text: So, where do skill, conditioning and tactics go in a session? A coach has ninety minutes. After the warm-up, there are three blocks to fit in: teaching a new skill, a hard conditioning block, and tactics for defending a set play. Write down the order you'd use, and the reason for your first decision. Then the harder part. What would you lose by putting conditioning first, and is that loss physical, technical, or both?

scenes.title: skill goes early, and judge it by next week

voiceover.text: Skill work goes early, after the warm-up and before heavy conditioning, and the reason isn't tradition. Learning a movement depends on the quality of each repetition, and quality falls with fatigue. A tired athlete moves slower and less precisely, so late practice can rehearse the compensations fatigue causes, not the technique you want. And a new skill needs most of the athlete's attention, which is limited. In Year 11 you met practice types, and the key finding: practice that looks worse in training often works better in games. So skill instruction, explaining, showing and correcting, is judged by what the athlete can do next week under pressure, not by how the drill looked today.

scenes.title: conditioning, and what its placement costs

voiceover.text: Conditioning builds the fitness the sport needs, with the methods and principles from earlier. Inside a session, the question is where it goes, and what that costs. Put it first, and conditioning gets the fresh athlete, but the skill and tactics after it are done tired and learned poorly. That's only worth it when the conditioning itself must be maximal, like top-speed sprinting. Put it last, and skill and tactics get the fresh athlete, while conditioning is done a bit tired. That's the default. Or build it into the skill work, so the athlete practises the skill as tired as a game makes them. A netballer who shoots well rested but misses in the last quarter needs exactly that, but only once the technique is stable. And with a squad, the same conditioning is too easy for some and too hard for others. So keep the structure, and vary the dose.

scenes.title: strategies and tactics, trained by decisions

voiceover.text: A strategy is the overall plan for a contest. A tactic is a specific action that carries it out in a given moment. A tennis player's strategy might be attacking the opponent's second serve. The tactic is stepping inside the baseline on that point. Students lose marks by mixing them up. "Our tactic was to play possession all match" describes a strategy. And tactics are trained by decisions, not explanations. A coach can describe a defensive structure in two minutes, but players still can't do it, because the hard part is spotting the cue under pressure and choosing. So tactical blocks use constraints: a smaller space, an overload like four against two, points only for a certain move, or a limit on touches, so the decision keeps happening. For one athlete, tactics are rehearsed alone against a model of the opponent. For a team, they need enough players and space, and shared communication.

The session closes with athlete reflection and coach evaluation, and they're not the same job. Reflection asks: what happened for me, why, and what will I change? It uses inside information no observer has, how the movement felt, and it builds ownership. It fails when it becomes a ritual, or is just about whether they won. Evaluation asks: did the session achieve its aim, and what should the next one contain? It uses outside evidence, like observation, data and whether the target behaviour happened. It fails when a session is judged by how busy it looked or how hard it felt. That's why the goal-specific aim from last time matters. Evaluation is a comparison against the aim. One athlete can reflect and be evaluated continuously. A squad needs a deliberate structure, or the quieter players never say anything.

Put the two videos together and a session has a default order: aim, safety, warm-up, skill, tactics, conditioning, cool-down, then reflection and evaluation. It comes from two facts: quality falls with fatigue, and attention is limited. Breaking the order needs a reason stronger than both. Now compare. Skill: continuous feedback for one athlete, sampled for a squad, because attention is divided. Conditioning: a dose set from one athlete's testing, against one structure with varied doses, because of many needs. Tactics: self-directed for one, collective for a team. Reflection: continuous for one, structured for a squad. And say what's the same: the order and its reasons, fatigue against learning, and evaluating against the aim.
Two things to remember. Skill fresh, fatigue last. And strategy is the plan, tactics are the moves.

Two exam questions. First. Here's a ninety-minute hockey plan, three days before a match, with its aim, on screen. Identify three problems and fix each, then explain why the aim can't be evaluated. Pause here to answer.

Conditioning comes before the new skill, so the skill is learned tired: move it after skill and tactics, and lighter. The tactics are explained, not trained: use a game with constraints that force the press. And there's no cool-down or evaluation: add both. The aim can't be evaluated, because it names no quality and no measure. The classic mistake is listing problems without fixes.

scenes.title: attempt two (the squad that holds the ball)

voiceover.text: Second. A netball squad keeps losing possession because players hold the ball too long before passing. Design a tactical block to fix this, explain why it works better than a whiteboard talk, and say how the coach should evaluate it. Pause here to answer.

Use a game with a constraint, like a ten-second clock to get the ball into the circle, in a smaller space. That makes the early decision happen again and again, under pressure, which a talk can't do. Evaluate against a goal-specific aim, like possessions lost from holding, counted in games before and after. The classic mistake is evaluating by how the drill looked.

So keep skill fresh, train tactics through decisions, pay the fatigue cost last, and close by reflecting and evaluating against the aim. That's one session. But a season has hundreds, and they can't all look the same. Shrink this one down, and it becomes one square in a year. How do you plan a whole training year?
